problem: The derivation of the same-layer spacing rule is technically wrong. It says two shapes on the same layer must be separated by 'more than twice the sideways etch plus Δ', where Δ is mask misalignment. Shapes on the same layer come from the same mask, so they shift together; misalignment between masks changes overlap and enclosure between different layers, not the gap between two shapes on one mask. The section also states that etch bias always makes gaps wider, which is only one sign of the bias; in the worst case each shape prints larger and the gap shrinks.
fix: Two shapes on the same mask move together, so mask misalignment does not change their spacing. The spacing rule guards against variation in printed size: if each edge of a shape can move outward by δ (resist and etch bias, lithography variation, either sign), a gap shrinks by 2δ, so minimum spacing must exceed 2δ. Misalignment Δ enters only the rules between different layers, which is why overlap and enclosure must exceed Δ.

problem: The answer says 'Mask misalignment and sideways etch can close a narrow gap'. Misalignment cannot close a gap between two shapes on the same layer, because both shapes are printed by the same mask and shift together.
fix: The gap can close because each of the two shapes may print wider than drawn (resist and etch bias, lithographic variation). If each edge can move outward by δ, the gap loses 2δ, so the minimum spacing keeps a margin larger than that worst-case closing. Misalignment is handled by overlap and enclosure rules between different layers.

problem: 'A metal wire is 20 squares long' treats squares as a length unit; the number of squares is a count, not a length.
fix: A metal wire has 20 squares, on a layer with sheet resistance 0.08 Ω per square.
